summary: For ages 7–9: observe that some materials change state when heated or cooled, and pin each change to a MEASURED temperature in °C (pure water melts/freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure). Core skill is observe-and-measure: read a thermometer and record the temperature where a change happens. Some mixtures, such as chocolate, soften and melt over a range of temperatures rather than at one sharp point. Keep melting distinct from dissolving, keep to physical reversible changes (avoid burning/cooking), and show that melting and freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. Particle-level 'why' is a light bridge, not the core.
misconceptions: Confusing melting with dissolving (thinking ice in a drink 'dissolves', or that melting needs a liquid to melt into).
Believing melting/boiling temperatures are vague or variable for a given substance, rather than fixed (water always 0°C / 100°C at normal pressure).
Thinking 'cold' is a substance that flows into things, rather than cooling being the removal of heat energy.
Assuming heating always makes new materials (over-generalising to chemical change) instead of many heating/cooling changes being reversible state changes.
Thinking a material must 'soften' gradually with no particular temperature, missing the idea of a specific melting point.

activities.title: Heat-and-cool bench: watch the change track the temperature
steps: Drag a heat dial under a beaker of ice and watch a thermometer climb in °C.

Notice the ice stays solid as the temperature rises, and observe that it begins to melt at 0°C, with a marker snapping onto the scale at that reading; the reading holds at 0°C while there is still ice melting.
Keep heating: once all the ice has melted the water warms to 100°C, where the reading holds while the water boils, with a marker at 100°C.
Reverse the dial to cool: watch steam recondense and the water refreeze at 0°C, showing the change runs both ways.
Use a side panel to run melting ice next to dissolving sugar and describe how the two processes differ.
Swap the material (chocolate, iron, oxygen) to discover each has its own change temperature or range (chocolate softens and melts gradually over a range of temperatures, not at one sharp point).
activities.insight: For water, melting, freezing and boiling do not happen vaguely 'when it gets warm': they happen at specific, readable temperatures (0°C and 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure) that are the same every time. The reading pauses at that temperature while the change is happening, and melting/freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. (Evaporation is different: it can happen slowly at temperatures below boiling.)

activities.title: Real thermometer in melting ice: predict the sticking point
steps: Put a thermometer into a beaker of crushed melting ice (a genuine ice-and-water mixture), stir gently and let it warm slowly (for example in a warm room or with gentle warming), reading the temperature aloud.
Before starting, predict what the thermometer does WHILE the ice is still melting, and say why.
Observe whether the reading climbs steadily or sticks, and record the temperature where it holds.
Afterwards, refreeze the melt-water and check it is the same water (e.g. mass stays the same if the container is covered so no water evaporates).
activities.insight: While a melting ice-and-water mixture still has ice in it the temperature holds at about 0°C (the energy first goes into changing state), then climbs once all the ice has melted; the melt-water is the same material as the ice.

activities.title: Melting is not dissolving — and freezing is heat leaving
steps: Compare ice melting in a warm room with sugar dissolving in water, and say what is different about each.
State which process needs heat and which needs a second substance.
Explain what happens when water freezes: does cold go IN, or does heat come OUT?
Decide whether melted chocolate is a new material or the same chocolate.
activities.insight: Melting is a heat-driven change of state of ONE substance; dissolving spreads a solid into a second liquid and does not need heating (though warming can speed it up). Freezing is heat energy leaving, not 'cold' moving in; a melted material is still the same material.

activities.title: Every material has its own change temperatures
steps: Read a table of materials and their change temperatures (water, chocolate, iron, oxygen).
Note that iron melts very hot and oxygen condenses very cold, while water melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C.
Place 0°C and 100°C correctly on a thermometer scale and read other values off it.
Match each state change (melting, freezing, boiling) to its temperature for water.
activities.insight: Each material has its own change temperatures. For pure substances like water these are specific readable values (at normal atmospheric pressure); some mixtures, like chocolate, melt over a range instead. Thermometer-reading is a real measurement skill.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: place the temperatures, tell the changes apart
steps: Place 0°C and 100°C on a thermometer scale.
Match each state change for water to its temperature (melt/freeze → 0°C, boil → 100°C).
Answer a question distinguishing melting from dissolving.
Sequence a heating timeline: ice → water → steam, with the temperature at each change point.
Explain whether melted ice is the same water, and give the reason.
activities.insight: The learner can state the fixed temperatures, keep melting distinct from dissolving, and explain change of state as the same material at a readable temperature.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Two children argue about melting ice. One says when ice melts it turns INTO a new liquid; the other says it's still exactly the same water, just changed state. Who is right, and why?' Then: 'At what temperature does ice melt, and what temperature does water boil?'
checkAnswer: It's the same water — melting is a change of STATE (solid to liquid), not a change into a new material; cooling reverses it back to ice. Ice melts at 0°C and water boils at 100°C. Heating adds energy so the particles move more and the solid becomes liquid.
